title: Class & the Codification of Manners
hook: Within a minute of meeting, strangers can guess each other's social class from how they listen, and the guess quietly decides who gets the job.
why:
Class is one of the least discussed and most powerful influences on how people are read. It is carried in accent and vocabulary, in how someone holds a knife and fork, in how they sit in an interview, in whether they nod eagerly or listen with cool detachment, in what they talk about when the work stops. Most people pick up these signals within seconds, rarely notice that they are doing so, and often mistake them for signs of character or ability.

For a man moving between worlds, from a working-class home to a university, from a trade to an office, from one country's class system to another's, these codes can feel like a test nobody announced. For a man in a position to judge others, they can quietly shape who seems polished, confident and right for the job.

This chapter covers how class is written on the body, how quickly it is read from behaviour and speech, how it shapes hiring through the idea of fit, how manners work as a gate, how to read without ranking, and what it means to move between worlds. It is about accuracy as much as fairness: ease is not competence, and eagerness is not weakness.

teach.h: Class is written on the body.
teach.p:
In 1979 the French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu argued that social class is carried not only in money and education but in the body. He called it habitus: the dispositions people absorb in childhood, which become second nature. How you sit, how loudly you speak, how much space you take, what you find funny, how you eat, what you wear and how you wear it all reflect where you grew up, and they feel to their owner like simply being natural.

Much of what counts as good manners was once deliberately codified. The sociologist Norbert Elias traced how European rules about eating with forks, using napkins, not spitting or blowing one's nose at the table spread from royal courts to the wealthy and then downward over several centuries. Each new rule became a way of telling who belonged.

The important point for a reader is that these habits are learned, not innate, and that they are learned unequally. A man who grew up with formal dinners, travel and professional parents absorbed one set of codes without effort. A man who grew up elsewhere absorbed different codes, just as complex and just as meaningful in their own setting, which may be misread or looked down on in another.

Reading class signals is therefore reading upbringing, not character. The figures here sit across a table, a setting where class is often most visible: in how people hold cutlery, pour drinks, use napkins and fill silences. None of it says anything about how clever, kind or capable either of them is.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if manners and bodily habits were innate rather than learned. Bourdieu's and Elias's work, and ordinary experience of how children absorb the habits of their homes, show them to be acquired.

teach.p:
In 2009 Michael Kraus and Dacher Keltner filmed pairs of strangers getting to know each other, then showed silent sixty-second clips to observers and asked them to estimate each person's social class. The observers' estimates agreed with each other, and they predicted the participants' actual family income and their mothers' education better than chance.

What were the observers picking up? The researchers coded the clips. Participants from wealthier, more educated backgrounds showed more signs of disengagement: doodling, grooming themselves, fiddling with objects nearby. Participants from poorer backgrounds showed more signs of engagement: nodding, laughing, raising their eyebrows, looking at their partner. The observers used these cues, mostly without knowing it.

Kraus and Keltner suggested an explanation. People with more resources depend less on others for help and can afford to attend less closely. People with fewer resources rely more on social ties and have learned to attend carefully to others. Neither style is better; each is adapted to a different life.

The trouble is how the styles are read. Detached ease tends to be read as confidence and status. Eager attentiveness can be read as nervousness, deference or lower status. The figure here leans back, at ease, one arm draped over a chair. In many rooms this posture reads as confidence. It may simply be a habit learned in a home where no one needed to watch anyone closely.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if observers could not estimate social class from short silent clips. Kraus and Keltner found that their estimates predicted family income and maternal education, through cues of engagement and disengagement.
teach.pullQuote: Ease is not competence, and eagerness is not weakness.

teach.p:
Speech carries class even more strongly than posture. In 2019 Michael Kraus and his colleagues found that listeners could judge a speaker's social class better than chance after hearing just seven words, read aloud out of context. Pronunciation carried more of the information than the choice of words.

The researchers then took the finding into hiring. They recorded real candidates for a laboratory job describing themselves briefly, then asked hundreds of people with hiring experience to evaluate them from the recordings. Candidates who sounded higher class were judged more competent and a better fit for the job, and were offered higher starting salaries and bonuses, though the evaluators knew nothing about their qualifications.

Part I's chapter on the voice described how quickly people judge others from speech. This study shows one of the most consequential directions those judgments take. An accent that signals a working-class or regional background can cost a candidate money and opportunity before they have said anything about their work.

The remedy for evaluators is the one Part IV recommended for interviews: structure. Decide in advance what a good answer contains, and score the content of what people say rather than how they sound. The figure here sits upright and still, the kind of quiet presence whose voice, once he speaks, will be judged in seconds.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if listeners could not judge class from brief speech, or if those judgments had no effect on hiring. Kraus and colleagues found both: class was detected from seven words, and higher-class speakers were judged more competent and offered more money.

teach.p:
In 2012 the sociologist Lauren Rivera published a study of hiring at elite investment banks, law firms and consulting firms in the United States. She interviewed 120 people who made hiring decisions and observed a hiring committee at work.

She found that evaluators placed great weight on what they called fit: whether a candidate was someone they would enjoy spending long hours with. In practice, fit often meant similarity. Evaluators warmed to candidates who shared their leisure pursuits, such as particular sports or travel, and their style of self-presentation. Some described warming to a candidate on discovering a shared sport. Rivera found that concerns about this kind of cultural similarity often outweighed concerns about how productive a candidate would be.

The leisure pursuits and styles that signalled fit were, Rivera noted, closely tied to wealth and upbringing: expensive sports, unpaid internships, travel, a certain polish in conversation. Fit, in other words, often reproduced class.

For anyone who interviews, the lesson is to notice when liking someone is doing the work that evidence should do. Ask about the work rather than hobbies. Be wary of the warm feeling of recognition, which is often a reading of shared background. The figure here sits with arms folded, leaning back, the posture of an interviewer who has already half decided, perhaps because the candidate reminded him of himself.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if evaluators at elite firms judged candidates mainly on likely performance rather than similarity. Rivera found that cultural similarity, including shared leisure pursuits, often outweighed concerns about productivity.

teach.p:
Manners work as a gate in many settings beyond hiring: client dinners, weddings, clubs, university halls, networking events. The rules are rarely stated. Which glass is yours, when to start eating, how to hold a wine glass, what counts as small talk, how to dress for a stated or unstated code, whether to shake hands or kiss on the cheek.

People who grew up with these codes follow them without effort, which makes them invisible. People who did not have to learn them in public, often under scrutiny, while trying to concentrate on the conversation. Many describe the experience vividly: watching others to see which fork to use, feeling their accent sharpen when nervous, wondering whether a joke will land, sensing a small pause when they do something different.

That effort shows. Someone working hard to follow unfamiliar codes may seem stiff, quiet, careful or uncomfortable. A reader who does not consider class may read that discomfort as shyness, coldness or lack of ability. The effort is the same kind described earlier in this part as masking: real, tiring and invisible to those who do not need to make it.

The kindest response is not to notice. Do not correct someone's manners in front of others, do not comment on an accent, and do not treat a different style as an error. The figure here sits with hands clasped in his lap, careful and still, the posture of someone watching the table for clues.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people from different class backgrounds found unfamiliar social codes equally easy. People who have moved between classes consistently describe the effort of learning codes others absorbed in childhood.

teach.p:
Reading class signals is unavoidable; ranking people by them is a choice. Almost everyone notices accent, clothing and manner within seconds, and noticing is not the problem. The problem begins when those signals are allowed to decide. A few practices help keep the two apart.

First, separate manner from merit. Ease, polish, a particular accent and a confident lean-back tell you about upbringing. They do not tell you about intelligence, skill, honesty or effort. Eager nodding, a regional accent and careful formality tell you the same kind of thing, in the other direction.

Second, use structure wherever decisions matter. Part IV's chapter on interviews described the evidence that structured interviews, with set questions and scored answers, predict performance better than open conversations. They also reduce the room for class signals to stand in for evidence.

Third, read your own warm and cool reactions as data about yourself. If you feel at ease with someone, ask whether it is because of what they said or because they reminded you of people you grew up with. If you feel faint discomfort, ask whether it comes from anything they did or simply from difference. The figure here takes notes, head down, the posture of an evaluator recording what was said rather than how it sounded.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if structured evaluation made no difference to the influence of class signals. Structure directs attention to the content of answers, leaving less room for accent and manner to stand in for evidence.

teach.p:
Many readers of this book will have moved between class worlds: the first in their family at university, a tradesman who became a manager, a man who married into a different background, an immigrant learning a new country's codes. Moving between worlds often means carrying two sets of habits and switching between them.

That switching is a skill, and also a cost. A later chapter in this part looks at code-switching in detail. Here, two points are worth making. First, the habits of your first world are not errors to be corrected. The attentiveness, warmth and directness many working-class men grow up with are assets in most rooms. Second, it is worth deciding consciously which codes you adopt and which you keep, rather than letting discomfort decide for you.

If you are now in a position to help others make the same move, the most useful thing you can do is explain the unwritten rules out loud and in private. Tell a new colleague how the client dinner will work, which conversations to expect, what the dress code really means. Codes that are explained lose much of their power to exclude.

The figures here work side by side on a shared task, one showing the other how something is done. Much of class mobility depends on someone being willing to show the rules rather than test for them.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if explaining unwritten rules made no difference to newcomers. People who move between class worlds consistently describe being shown the codes, rather than left to guess them, as a decisive help.

poseGallery.annotation: Ease tells you about upbringing. Score the content of answers, not how relaxed someone looks saying them.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Correcting someone's manners in front of others

caseStudy:
Charles, fifty-two, is a partner at a consulting firm and regularly interviews graduates. Last year he saw two candidates on the same afternoon. The first, Hugo, was relaxed and articulate, had rowed at university and spent a summer interning at a bank his uncle worked for. They talked about Italy for ten minutes. The second, Danny, had worked in a warehouse through university, spoke with a strong Liverpool accent, nodded a great deal and laughed nervously at Charles's jokes.

Charles's instinct was clear: Hugo was a natural. But the firm had recently introduced structured interviews, and when Charles scored both candidates against the set questions, Danny's answers to the case problem were noticeably stronger. Charles looked at his notes and realised that most of what he had liked about Hugo was how familiar he felt. Hugo's answers had been fluent but thin; Danny's had been hesitant at the start and then precise, with numbers, a clear structure and a sensible recommendation.

The firm hired Danny. Before his first client dinner, Charles took him aside and explained how the evening would go: who would be there, what they would talk about, how the bill would be handled, what to wear. Danny said later that it was the most useful thing anyone had told him in his first year.

Charles has started paying attention to the moment of recognition in interviews, the feeling that a candidate is someone like him, and treating it as a reason to check his scores rather than as evidence.
observe: Notice, in your next meeting with someone new, whether you feel at ease or slightly uncomfortable, and what in their manner or speech prompted it.
Notice cues of engagement and disengagement in a group: who nods and laughs, who doodles or leans back, and how each is being read.
Notice accents in your workplace, and whether some are associated with particular roles or levels of seniority.
Notice unwritten rules in a setting you know well, such as a client dinner or a club, and which of them a newcomer would have to guess.

drills.name: Ease Versus Evidence
steps: Think of someone you rated highly in a first meeting.
List what made the impression: what they said, and how they said it.
Separate the two columns: content and manner.
Ask whether your impression would survive if you had only the content.

drills.name: Name the Hidden Rules
steps: Choose a setting you know well: a client dinner, a team social, a formal event.
Write down ten unwritten rules a newcomer would need to know.
Mark which ones you learned without being told.
Share the list, privately and kindly, with someone new to that setting.

drills.name: Score the Content
steps: Before your next interview or assessment, write down what a strong answer to each question would contain.
During the conversation, note what was said, in the candidate's words.
Score against your list before forming an overall impression.
Compare your scores with your gut feeling, and note where they differ.

drills.name: Accent Check
steps: Listen to a few voices you hear this week: colleagues, callers, people on television.
Notice any assumption you form about each speaker's intelligence or competence from their accent.
Ask what evidence you actually have for it.
Write one sentence about what you noticed.

quiz.q: A manager says the candidate who leaned back, relaxed and unhurried, clearly has the most confidence and ability. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since relaxed ease in an interview reliably signals both competence and real confidence in the work
Relaxed disengagement is linked to class background, not ability, so it should not stand in for evidence
Leaning back always signals arrogance, so the candidate should be marked down for showing it
Interview posture is random and says nothing about anything, including where someone grew up
quiz.explain: Kraus and Keltner found that people from wealthier backgrounds showed more disengagement cues. Ease is a habit learned in a particular upbringing, not a measure of ability.

quiz.q: What did Kraus and Keltner find in their 2009 study of strangers getting acquainted?
options: Wealthier participants showed more disengagement, poorer participants more nods and laughs
Wealthier participants nodded and laughed more, while poorer participants doodled and fidgeted
There were no differences in behaviour between participants from different backgrounds
Observers could not estimate anyone's class from the clips, whatever cues were present
quiz.explain: Participants from wealthier backgrounds doodled, groomed and fiddled more, while those from poorer backgrounds nodded, laughed and looked at their partner more. Observers used these cues to estimate class better than chance.

quiz.q: What did Kraus and colleagues find in their 2019 study of speech and hiring?
options: Listeners needed several minutes of speech before they could judge anyone's class
Evaluators preferred working-class speakers, judging them more honest and hardworking
Class was judged from seven words, and higher-class speakers were offered more money
Word choice mattered far more than pronunciation in judging a speaker's class
quiz.explain: Listeners judged class from just seven words, mostly from pronunciation. Evaluators rated higher-class-sounding candidates as more competent and offered them higher salaries, without knowing their qualifications.

quiz.q: According to Rivera's study of elite firms, what did evaluators often mean by fit?
options: How well a candidate's qualifications matched the job description
How quickly a candidate could be trained to do the specific work required
How well a candidate would represent the firm's values to clients
Similarity to themselves, including shared leisure pursuits and style
quiz.explain: Fit often meant cultural similarity, including sports, travel and self-presentation, and it often outweighed concerns about productivity. Because those pursuits track wealth, fit tended to reproduce class.

quiz.q: At a client dinner, a new junior colleague uses his cutlery and napkin differently from everyone else. What fits this chapter best?
options: Say nothing at the table, and offer to explain the dinner codes privately if he wants
Correct him quietly at the table, so that the clients do not notice the mistake
Make a light joke about it, so that he knows nobody minds and can relax
Mention it to his manager afterwards, so that he can be given some training
quiz.explain: A different style is not an error, and public correction adds to the effort he is already making. Explaining unwritten rules privately, if he wants it, helps without humiliating.

quiz.q: You interviewed two candidates. One was polished and easy to talk to; the other was nervous, with a strong regional accent, but gave stronger answers. What fits this chapter best?
options: Hire the polished candidate, since clients will respond better to his manner
Score both against the criteria you set in advance, and decide on the answers
Hire the nervous candidate, since accents should always be favoured in hiring
Ask both back for a second, informal interview over lunch to see who fits in
quiz.explain: Structured scoring directs attention to what was said rather than how it sounded. An informal lunch would give class signals even more room to stand in for evidence.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific moment when class shaped how you read someone, or how you were read: an interview, a dinner, a first day, a meeting with in-laws. Describe the signals involved: accent, manners, posture, clothing, the topics of conversation. What conclusion was drawn, and was it about upbringing or about ability? If you have moved between class worlds yourself, describe one code you had to learn, and one habit from your first world you have chosen to keep.
reflection.guidance: Class is rarely discussed openly, so it can take a moment to see it. Focus on specific behaviours rather than general impressions, and be honest about both directions: the times you were judged and the times you judged others. If nothing comes to mind, think about the last time someone's accent or table manners surprised you, and what you assumed about them in that first moment.

failureMode: The first failure is to read ease and polish as competence, when they mostly reflect upbringing. The second is to read eager attentiveness, nodding and laughing as nervousness or low status. The third is to judge people by accent, when class can be heard in seven words and costs candidates money. The fourth is to hire for fit, when fit often means similarity to yourself. The fifth is to correct someone's manners in front of others or treat a different style as an error. And the sixth, for those who have moved between worlds, is to treat the habits of your first world as faults to be erased rather than assets to keep.

watch.title: Titanic: First Class Dinner
watch.notice: A steerage passenger at a first-class dinner. Notice how he watches the others for the codes, how the diners read his manners, and how much of the scene is about cutlery, posture and timing rather than words.

watch.title: Parasite: Official Trailer
watch.notice: A poor family infiltrates a wealthy household. Notice the small physical giveaways of class the film turns on: posture, manners and, famously, smell, and how carefully the family performs the codes of the house.
